Optional workflow B needs another 14 hours. Another engineer's hours consume the same funded cap. No scope change exists. Return answer as {"remaining_hours":int,"a_hours":int,"after_a_hours":int,"a_plus_b_shortfall":int,"a_fits":bool,"both_fit":bool}. Explain the funding/staffing distinction.

In a fictional report pipeline, 1% of reports contain a material error. Two alarms are conditionally independent given whether a report has an error. Each alarm fires on 90% of erroneous reports and on 5% of clean reports. Both alarms fired on one report. Releasing it costs $100 if erroneous and $0 otherwise. Perfect manual review costs $8 and prevents the error cost. No other costs apply. Return answer as {"error_posterior":number,"release_expected_cost":number,"review_expected_cost":number,"decision":"review" or "release"}. Give probabilities as decimals and money in dollars; absolute tolerance 0.00001. Explain how conditional independence is used; do not assume unconditional independence.

answers.answer_text: {"answer":{"error_posterior":0.7659574468,"release_expected_cost":76.5957446809,"review_expected_cost":8,"decision":"review"},"explanation":"Conditional independence applies only after conditioning on report status: P(both alarms|error)=0.9×0.9=0.81 and P(both alarms|clean)=0.05×0.05=0.0025. Bayes’ rule gives P(error|both)=0.01×0.81/(0.01×0.81+0.99×0.0025)=0.7659574468. Thus releasing has expected cost $100×0.7659574468=$76.5957446809, while perfect review costs $8 and prevents the error cost. Review is cheaper."}

{"answer":{"error_posterior":0.7659574468,"release_expected_cost":76.5957446809,"review_expected_cost":8,"decision":"review"},"explanation":"Conditional independence gives P(both alarms | error) = 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 and P(both alarms | clean) = 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025. Bayes' rule gives an error posterior of (0.01 × 0.81)/(0.01 × 0.81 + 0.99 × 0.0025) = 36/47. Release costs $100 times this probability in expectation, while perfect review costs only $8 and prevents the error cost. Thus review is cheaper. Unconditional independence is not assumed."}

Assign seven indivisible jobs J1..J7 to machines A, B, C. Each job goes entirely to exactly one machine. Capacities are A=8, B=7, C=5 units. Job demands are J1=4, J2=3, J3=2, J4=2, J5=1, J6=1, J7=1. Opening a used machine costs A=$6, B=$4, C=$5, charged once; unused machines cost nothing. The table gives each job's TOTAL assignment cost (not per-unit):
job | A | B | C
J1 | 4 | 8 | 6
J2 | 7 | 3 | 5
J3 | 5 | 4 | 2
J4 | 2 | 5 | 4
J5 | 4 | 1 | 3
J6 | 3 | 4 | 1
J7 | 2 | 2 | 4
J1 and J2 must use different machines. J3 and J4 must use the same machine. Minimize assignment costs plus opening costs. Among minimum-cost assignments, choose the lexicographically smallest machine sequence for J1..J7, with A<B<C. Return answer as {"machines":[seven strings],"total_cost":integer,"loads":{"A":int,"B":int,"C":int}}. Explain why the assignment is feasible and why a cheaper one is excluded; no tools.

answers.answer_text: {"answer":{"machines":["A","B","A","A","B","B","B"],"total_cost":31,"loads":{"A":8,"B":6,"C":0}},"explanation":"J3 and J4 share A. Loads are A: 4+2+2=8, B: 3+1+1+1=6, C: 0, so capacities hold, and J1 and J2 differ. Assignment cost is 4+3+5+2+1+4+2=21; opening A and B costs 10, totaling 31. Treating J3/J4 as one demand-4 block, exhaustive feasible placement by ordered (J1,J2) machine pair gives minimum totals: (A,B)=31, (A,C)=35, (B,A)=38, (B,C)=39, (C,A)=39, (C,B)=35. Thus no cheaper assignment exists. The cost-31 assignment is unique, so it is also lexicographically smallest."}

{"answer":{"machines":["A","B","A","A","B","B","B"],"total_cost":31,"loads":{"A":8,"B":6,"C":0}},"explanation":"Loads are A=8, B=6, C=0, within capacity. J1 and J2 differ; J3 and J4 share A. Assignment costs total $21 and opening costs $10. Total demand is 14, so feasible solutions must use A+B or all three machines; other machine subsets lack capacity. Using all three costs at least $15 opening plus assignment lower bound 4+3+6+1+1+2=$17, hence at least $32. Using only A+B: if J3/J4 use A, the minimum total is $31 with J1 on A, or $38 with J1 on B. If J3/J4 use B, capacity forces J1 onto A and J2 onto B, giving $35. The $31 case fills A with J1/J3/J4, forcing every remaining job onto B. Thus this optimum is unique and therefore lexicographically smallest."}
